blocks.prompt: The Pouch That Faces the Wrong Way
blocks.text: A wombat is a marsupial from Australia. That means it carries its baby in a pouch. Most pouches open at the top. A wombat's pouch opens toward its back legs. That sounds strange until you watch a wombat dig. Dirt flies backward past the pouch instead of into it, so the baby stays clean and safe. Wombats dig with claws like little shovels. They make tunnels called burrows. A burrow can be longer than a school bus and can have many doors. The wombat sleeps down there all day, where it is cool and dark. At night it comes out and eats grass for hours.

blocks.prompt: A Pile of Dice on a Rock
blocks.text: If you found a small pile of cubes on top of a rock in an Australian field, you might think someone dropped a set of dice. You did not. You found wombat poop. A wombat is a stocky, burrowing marsupial about the size of a large dog. It spends the day asleep in a tunnel it dug itself and comes out at night to eat grass. It cannot see very well, so it finds its way by smell. That is where the cubes come in. Wombats leave their droppings in high places: on a rock, on a log, on a mound of dirt at the edge of their patch. The message is simple. This is my ground. A round dropping would roll off the rock and land in the grass, where nobody would notice it. A cube stays put. For a long time, nobody knew how an animal could make a cube. Scientists guessed the wombat had a square opening, which is not true. The answer was hiding somewhere else, deep inside the wombat, and it took a team with a very unusual research project to find it.

blocks.prompt: Cubes, Bulldozers, and a Backside Made of Armor
blocks.text: Australia has three kinds of wombat, and all of them are built like small bulldozers. A wombat stands low to the ground, weighs as much as a big dog, and carries claws that work like garden trowels. It digs burrows that can run a hundred feet through the soil, with side rooms and several exits. Down there the air stays cool and still, which matters in a country that gets brutally hot. The wombat's body is a set of solutions to living underground and eating poorly. Grass is tough, dry, and low in energy, so the wombat treats every mouthful with patience. Food can take about two weeks to pass through its gut, one of the slowest digestions of any mammal. Almost every drop of water gets pulled back out along the way. Its teeth never stop growing, because grass full of grit would wear ordinary teeth down to nothing. Even its pouch is engineered. A kangaroo's pouch opens upward. A wombat's opens toward its tail, so that when the mother throws dirt backward with her front claws, the joey inside stays clean. Then there is the backside. The bones at the end of a wombat's spine are fused into a plate, and the skin and cartilage over it are thick and tough. When something chases a wombat, it dives headfirst into its burrow and jams that armored rump into the opening like a cork. A dingo at the entrance finds nothing soft to bite. And in the morning, on a rock near the burrow, the wombat leaves a neat stack of cubes. No other animal on Earth makes a cube. For years, nobody could explain how this one does.

blocks.prompt: The Only Cube in Nature
blocks.text: Nothing else in the living world makes a cube. Crystals grow into cubes, but crystals are not alive. Every animal that has ever been studied produces droppings that are round, tubular, or shapeless, because a soft material squeezed through a round tube comes out round. The bare-nosed wombat of Australia is the single exception, and for decades that fact sat in the textbooks with no explanation attached to it. The wombat had reasons to be strange. It is a burrowing marsupial that survives on grass so poor in energy that it must digest each meal for around two weeks, one of the slowest guts of any mammal. It lives in dry country, so its intestine, roughly as long as a school bus, strips out nearly every drop of water before the waste reaches the end. By the time the material arrives it is not sloppy. It is stiff, dry, and ready to hold a shape. That still leaves the question of why cubes are worth making. A wombat cannot see well. It reads its world by scent, and it advertises its territory by leaving droppings in the most obvious place available: on top of a rock, a log, or a mound at a burrow entrance. Height carries scent. A round dropping placed on a rock rolls off and vanishes into the grass. A cube sits where it is put. The shape is not decoration. It is a solution to a problem of publishing. The mechanism stayed hidden until a team of engineers and a wildlife ecologist decided the question deserved real equipment. Patricia Yang, then at Georgia Tech, worked with Scott Carver in Tasmania on intestines from wombats that had died on roads. They inflated the tissue and measured how much each part of the wall could stretch. The result was a surprise. The wombat's intestine is not the same all the way around. Near the end, two narrow strips of the wall are stiff and grooved while the rest is springy. As the muscles squeeze the drying contents along that final stretch, the springy parts bulge outward and the stiff strips hold their line, and the material is slowly pressed into a shape with flat faces and rounded corners. No square opening. No mold. Just a tube that is deliberately uneven. The work won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2019, an award for research that makes people laugh and then makes them think. The thinking part matters. Human factories make cubes by cutting them out or by pouring material into molds. A wombat makes about a hundred a night with nothing but soft tissue and rhythm, and engineers who design with soft materials would very much like to know how.

blocks.prompt: The Wombat's Cube: What a Strange Question Was Worth
blocks.text: For most of the twentieth century, the wombat's cube was a curiosity that nobody in science was willing to spend money on. The fact itself was never in doubt. Anyone who has walked a paddock in Tasmania has seen the evidence: small dry blocks, roughly three quarters of an inch across, stacked on a rock or a fallen branch like a game abandoned halfway through. It was simply assumed that some quiet anatomical accident produced them, and that the accident was not important. Both assumptions turned out to be wrong. Start with the animal. The bare-nosed wombat is a marsupial engineered from the ground down. It weighs up to about seventy pounds, moves on short powerful legs, and digs with claws that shift soil the way a small excavator does. Its burrows can run a hundred feet and branch into chambers. Its rearmost vertebrae are fused into a bony plate covered by thick hide and cartilage, so that when a dingo gives chase the wombat dives into its tunnel and plugs the entrance with a backside that offers nothing worth biting. Its pouch faces backward, away from the spray of dirt it throws while digging. Every one of these features answers a question the environment asked. Its digestion answers the hardest question of all. Australian grasses are dry, tough, and thin on nutrition, and the wombat's response is patience taken to an extreme. A meal spends roughly two weeks inside it, one of the slowest passages measured in any mammal. Along a gut that would stretch about thirty feet if pulled straight, water is reclaimed almost completely, because in that country water is the currency that runs out first. The consequence is that the waste reaching the final stretch of intestine is unusually dry and stiff. It behaves less like paste and more like clay. Now the question of why. The wombat's eyesight is poor and its territory is invisible, so it communicates by scent, and scent travels best from height. The animal deposits its droppings on rocks, logs, and mounds at burrow entrances, where the smell can carry. A round dropping on a rock does what round things do on slopes. It rolls off, disappears into the grass, and says nothing to anyone. A cube stays where it is placed. Shape, in other words, is the message getting delivered rather than lost. The mechanism resisted explanation until Patricia Yang, an engineer studying fluid mechanics at Georgia Tech, heard about the cubes and refused to let the question go. Working with Scott Carver, a wildlife ecologist at the University of Tasmania, she examined intestines from wombats killed on roads. The team inflated sections of the tissue and measured how far each part of the wall would stretch. The wall, it emerged, is not the same all the way around. In the last portion of the intestine, two narrow strips are stiff and grooved while the surrounding tissue is elastic. Over roughly the final tenth of the journey, the muscular squeezing of the gut works the drying contents against those uneven walls: the elastic regions push outward and shape the faces, the stiff strips hold the corners. There is no square opening at the end. There is no mold. There is a tube that is intentionally inconsistent, and time. In 2019 the finding won an Ig Nobel Prize, which honors research that first makes people laugh and then makes them think. It is easy to stop at the laugh. The thought underneath is this: human beings manufacture cubes by cutting a shape out of a larger piece or by pouring material into a mold, and both methods are wasteful and rigid. A wombat produces around a hundred cubes a night using soft tissue, muscular rhythm, and no tooling at all. Engineers who work with soft matter, from food to living tissue, have taken an interest for exactly that reason. The strange question was worth asking. The strange questions usually are.
